title: Ernesto "Che" Guevara
summary: Argentine-born physician who joined Fidel Castro's guerrillas, helped win the Cuban Revolution, held senior economic posts in Cuba, then led failed guerrilla expeditions in the Congo and Bolivia, where Bolivian soldiers executed him at La Higuera on 9 October 1967.
card: Born in Rosario in 1928, Ernesto Guevara trained as a doctor, lived through the 1954 coup in Guatemala, and sailed with Fidel Castro's expedition to Cuba in 1956. After the revolution's victory he ran the La Cabaña fortress prison, where the number of executions is disputed, and later served as bank president and industry minister. He left Cuba in 1965 for campaigns in the Congo and Bolivia that failed, and his death turned him into a contested symbol of revolution.
what:
Ernesto Guevara, known as Che, was born on 14 June 1928 in Rosario, Argentina, into a middle-class family and studied medicine in Buenos Aires, graduating in 1953. He travelled through South America in 1951–52, a journey that reference works describe as running north from Chile to Caracas, and reached Guatemala in December 1953. There he supported the reformist government of Jacobo Arbenz. Its overthrow on 27 June 1954, sponsored by the United States, pushed him towards armed revolution; he took refuge in the Argentine embassy and then moved to Mexico City, where he met Fidel and Raúl Castro in 1955.

He sailed with the 82 men of the Granma expedition, which landed in eastern Cuba on 2 December 1956. He began as the group's doctor, became commander of the second rebel column in the Sierra Maestra in 1957, and led the force that took Santa Clara at the end of 1958, where an armoured train surrendered on 30 December. Batista fled on 1 January 1959 and Guevara entered Havana the next day.

In 1959 he commanded La Cabaña fortress, where revolutionary tribunals sentenced and shot officials of the old regime and others. Cuba Archive documents 73 executions there between 4 January and 26 November 1959, while other writers cite figures from about 179 to 700, and sources disagree on how many he personally ordered. Cuba granted him citizenship on 9 January 1959. He then headed the industrial department of the agrarian reform institute, the National Bank, and, from 1961 to 1965, the Ministry of Industry. He addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 11 December 1964.

He resigned his posts in 1965 and led a Cuban column to the eastern Congo, which his own account called a failure; the group withdrew in November 1965. In November 1966 he entered Bolivia on a forged passport and built a guerrilla base in the Ñancahuazú region. Bolivian Rangers wounded and captured him on 8 October 1967, and he was shot at La Higuera the next day on the order of the Bolivian high command. His remains were identified in 1997 and reburied at Santa Clara, Cuba.

uncertainty.note: Birth (14 June 1928) and death (9 October 1967) are given consistently by the sources opened. The hour of death is not settled: a Bolivian communiqué of 16 October 1967 said about 8 p.m. on 8 October, General Ovando said 1:30 p.m. on 9 October, and Félix Rodríguez's CIA debriefing puts the shooting at 1:10 p.m. on 9 October (National Security Archive). Other 1950s-60s waypoint dates are given to the precision the sources support.

how: Guevara's path followed a chain of decisions and events rather than a single plan. A medical education and two years of travel led him to Guatemala, where the 1954 overthrow of Arbenz convinced him that reform could not survive against hostile great-power opposition. In Mexico he joined the Castros, sailed on the Granma, and survived the disaster that followed the landing to fight in the Sierra Maestra, rising to a column commander. After victory he held military, banking and industrial offices. In 1965 he resigned, tried to export the guerrilla model to the Congo, and then in 1966 to Bolivia, where a Ranger battalion operating under an April 1967 US Army agreement, with a CIA officer alongside, hunted his band down. Captured wounded on 8 October 1967, he was shot the next day.
why_it_matters: Guevara turned a national revolution into an international cause. His writings and example popularised the small armed band, the foco, as a route to power, and the Bolivian campaign showed its limit: an isolated rural band without local support was defeated by counter-insurgency-trained regular troops, a conclusion also drawn in later reference accounts of the campaign. His Congo expedition, studied by Piero Gleijeses as an act of Cuban state policy rather than personal adventure, preceded Cuba's far larger African deployments. In Cuba, the revolutionary tribunals he supervised at La Cabaña in 1959 and his later economic offices remain part of how the state and its critics argue about the revolution. After his death and the return of his remains in 1997, his image was claimed by very different groups: the Cuban state presents him as a model, admirers elsewhere as an idealist, critics as an ideologue. Had the 1954 coup in Guatemala not occurred, he might have stayed a physician in Central America; Castro himself tied Guevara's hatred of imperialism to that event, though that is a reading, not a certainty. Had Bolivian officers kept him alive, as Rodríguez says Washington wanted, a trial would have followed instead of a martyr's death.

perspectives.holder: Cuban state and admirers (Fidel Castro 1967; Yepe 2009)
perspectives.account: Guevara was a model revolutionary and humane physician who respected prisoners, a gifted military and economic leader and an internationalist whose example outlived him; Castro condemned the manner of his killing.

perspectives.holder: Cuba Archive and critical writers (Werlau; Vargas Llosa)
perspectives.account: As commander of La Cabaña and presiding over its appeal process in 1959 he bears responsibility for executions carried out without basic legal guarantees; Cuba Archive documents 123 cases attributed to him, and Vargas Llosa lists higher estimates up to 700 and notes that the larger figures may include executions after he left the post.

Admirers cite his idealism and courage and note his cult status among 1960s youth; detractors call him a bloodthirsty adventurer and a failure; the Bolivian campaign is also read as evidence that isolated rural guerrillas lose to trained counter-insurgency troops.

perspectives.holder: Participants in the capture (Félix Rodríguez, via CIA debriefing; Bolivian officers)
perspectives.account: Rodríguez said he was under instructions to keep Guevara alive but relayed the Bolivian high command's order to kill him; the Bolivian authorities first claimed he died of wounds in battle. These accounts are the participants' own and are not independently confirmed.

numbers.label: Documented executions at La Cabaña fortress prison, 4 January-26 November 1959
numbers.note: Cuba Archive count of people believed executed at La Cabaña; single figure because the source reports one running count and says the true number may never be known.

numbers.label: Higher published claims of executions at La Cabaña under Guevara, 1959
numbers.note: Vargas Llosa lists about 179 (Armando Lago, named victims), about 200 (Pedro Corzo), about 400 (a former tribunal lawyer, January-June 1959), over 500 (US embassy cables) and 700 (Castaneda citing a priest). He notes the larger figures may include executions after Guevara left the post. Claims, not agreed totals.

numbers.label: Cases of executions attributed to Guevara across Cuba, 1957-1959 (Cuba Archive, work in progress)
numbers.note: Single figure because the source gives one running count and says the true number may never be known.

numbers.label: Fighters aboard the Granma landing
numbers.note: Both the Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Cuban Insights give 82; some accounts give 81.

numbers.label: Rebel fighters under Guevara at Santa Clara
numbers.note: Approximate figure from a solidarity-campaign article and from Castro's 1967 speech (about 300); other accounts give different numbers. Opposing garrison reported as 3,500 plus about 400 on the armoured train.

numbers.label: Size of Guevara's Bolivian guerrilla band
numbers.note: NSA narrative says about sixty fighters; a June 1967 US White House memo put strength at 40-50; Rangers found seventeen guerrillas in the valley on 8 October 1967.

audience_note: Contains accounts of executions, including summary shootings at La Cabaña in 1959 and the killing of a wounded prisoner at La Higuera in 1967, and of the treatment of his body afterwards. A well-known photograph of his captors with him before his death is not embedded.

importance.justification: A defining figure of the Cold War in Latin America and Africa whose life path crosses three continents and whose image remains one of the most reproduced of the twentieth century.
